title: ENISA Threat Landscape 2025
source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: 4,875 EU incidents curated by ENISA analysts
cards.description: Across the 1 July 2024 – 30 June 2025 reporting period, ENISA analysts collected and curated 4,875 incidents impacting EU Member States and EU-based organisations, drawn primarily from open sources and ENISA Cyber Partnership Programme contributions.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Hacktivism reached 79% of total EU incidents
cards.description: Despite minimal real-world impact, hacktivist activity continued to dominate ENISA reporting, accounting for almost 80% of recorded incidents — driven primarily by ideology-motivated DDoS waves.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: DDoS dominates EU incident types at 76.7%
cards.description: The distribution of incident types in ENISA's EU dataset is dominated by DDoS attacks (about 76.7%), overwhelmingly driven by hacktivist groups, with cybercrime extortion-led ransom-DDoS playing a marginal role.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Phishing drives 60% of initial intrusions
cards.description: Social-engineering tactics remain the primary entry point for threat actors in the EU, with phishing (including vishing, malspam and malvertising) accounting for roughly 60% of observed intrusion-vector cases.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Vulnerability exploitation 21.3% of intrusions
cards.description: Exploitation of vulnerabilities remains a cornerstone of initial access (21.3%) in the EU dataset, with widespread campaigns weaponising newly disclosed flaws within days of publication.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Public administration is the top targeted sector (38%)
cards.description: Public administration remained the most targeted sector in the EU at 38% of incidents, with the increase primarily driven by hacktivist-led DDoS attacks against government websites and portals.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: AI-supported phishing tops 80% of social engineering
cards.description: By early 2025, AI-supported phishing campaigns reportedly represented more than 80% of observed social-engineering activity worldwide, with adversaries leveraging jailbroken LLMs, synthetic media and model-poisoning techniques.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Akira drives 48.7% of EU manufacturing ransomware
cards.description: Among ransomware strains deployed against EU manufacturing organisations, Akira dominated at 48.7%, followed by Qilin (20.5%) and FOG (10.3%), reinforcing Akira's status as a top-of-mind threat to industrial operators.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: 42,595 new vulnerabilities disclosed (+27% YoY)
cards.description: ENISA recorded 42,595 new vulnerabilities disclosed over the reporting period — a 27% rise on the prior year. CVSS triage showed 7% Critical, 26% High, 43% Medium, 3% Low and 21% unscored. The sparkline approximates the implied severity distribution.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Lumma stealer hit 394,000 Windows machines
cards.description: Assessed as the most prevalent info-stealer in 2025, Lumma was reportedly deployed on 394,000 Windows machines globally between March and May 2025, with strong prevalence in the EU before Europol-coordinated takedowns of ~2,300 malicious domains.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Shift toward mixed, convergent cyber pressure
cards.description: ENISA's headline narrative for 2025: the threat picture is shifting from rare high-impact events to a continuous, diversified campaign environment that steadily erodes EU resilience.
cards.quote: "The cyber threat landscape is shifting toward mixed, possibly convergent pressure, with fewer single high impact incidents, and more continuous, diversified and convergent campaigns that collectively erode resilience."
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Initial intrusion vectors in the EU
cards.description: Phishing dominates initial intrusion in ENISA's EU dataset, followed by exploitation of vulnerabilities, botnets, malicious applications and insider misuse — a mix that underscores the continued primacy of social engineering alongside technical exploitation.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Distribution of EU incident types
cards.description: DDoS attacks dwarf all other recorded incident categories in the EU dataset, followed by intrusions (cybercrime and state-aligned), with defacements remaining a small, almost exclusively hacktivist tactic.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Top five EU sectors targeted
cards.description: Once unspecified targeting is set aside, public administration far outstrips other verticals as the most targeted EU sector, followed by transport, digital infrastructure, finance and manufacturing. Essential entities under NIS2 represent 53.7% of all recorded incidents.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: EU member states with most public-administration hits
cards.description: Within the public-administration sector, France, Italy and Germany absorbed the highest recorded incident shares, followed by Spain and Poland — patterns shaped by hacktivist-led DDoS targeting governmental websites.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Top EU member states named in ransomware & breach claims
cards.description: Germany leads ransomware and data-breach claims affecting EU organisations at 23.4%, followed by Italy, Spain, France and Belgium — largely tracking each market's economic weight as a target of opportunity.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Most-deployed ransomware strains in the EU
cards.description: Ransomware activity in the EU has fragmented sharply post-LockBit. Akira leads at 11.6% of deployments, followed by SafePay and Qilin, illustrating a more evenly distributed but professionalised RaaS ecosystem.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity
cards.comparison: 82 ransomware variants observed against EU MSs

cards.title: Most active hacktivist groups against EU
cards.description: Pro-Russia NoName057(16) overwhelmingly dominates EU-targeted hacktivism at 63.1% of attacks, with Keymous+, Dark Storm Team, Mr Hamza and RipperSec rounding out the top five.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Hacktivist targeting by EU sector
cards.description: Hacktivist activity in the EU is heavily concentrated on public administration (63.1%), followed by transport, finance, digital infrastructure and a tie between manufacturing and media/entertainment.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Hacktivist attack mix is DDoS-first
cards.description: Within hacktivist activity targeting EU Member States, DDoS attacks account for 91.5% of incidents, with claimed intrusions at just 5.1% and data breaches at 3.4% — underscoring DDoS as a low-skill, high-visibility tactic.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: EU transport incidents concentrate in air and logistics
cards.description: Within the transport sector, ENISA records a concentration of incidents in air transport (58.4%) and logistics (20.8%) — reflecting both hacktivist DDoS waves and ransomware impacts on maritime, freight and airport operators.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Threat category mix across the EU
cards.description: ENISA's threat-category distribution highlights mobile threats as the largest share (42.4%), followed by web threats, operational-technology threats and supply-chain risks — evidence that attackers exploit both digital surfaces and indirect dependencies.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Adversary objectives behind EU incidents
cards.description: Most EU-targeting activity is ideology-driven (hacktivist DDoS), followed by financially motivated cybercrime, with state-aligned cyberespionage representing 7.2% but remaining a primary medium-to-long-term concern.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: CVSS severity breakdown of disclosed vulnerabilities
cards.description: Of the 42,595 vulnerabilities disclosed during the period, ENISA classifies 7% Critical, 26% High, 43% Medium, 3% Low and 21% unscored — highlighting both the volume and the triage backlog facing EU defenders.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Top Russia-aligned FIMI operators against the EU
cards.description: Out of 86 FIMI operations targeting EU entities and Member States captured by EEAS, Matryoshka led with 18 cases, followed by Doppelgänger, Storm-1516 and the Russian Foundation to Battle Injustice; Portal Kombat infrastructure was used in 19 cases to amplify content.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: State-aligned activity = 7.2% of EU incidents
cards.description: Between July 2024 and June 2025, 7.2% of recorded EU-targeted incidents were associated with state-aligned activities — led by Russia-nexus, then China-nexus and DPRK-nexus intrusion sets, plus emerging India-nexus targeting.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: 64% of CVEs are network-exploitable
cards.description: When considering the CVSS Attack Vector metric, 64% of newly documented vulnerabilities can be exploited over the network — underscoring the systemic risk posed by Internet-facing systems across EU organisations.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: 68.6% of intrusions ended in saleable data breaches
cards.description: Out of recorded intrusions in the EU, 68.6% resulted in data leaked or advertised on cybercriminal forums for sale (2.8% of those tied directly to a ransomware claim), while 30.2% led to data exfiltration including credential theft and strategic collection.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity

cards.title: Ransomware, banking trojans & infostealers = 87.3% of post-intrusion code
cards.description: Combined, ransomware, banking trojans and infostealers account for 87.3% of malicious code observed after EU intrusions — cementing the financially motivated cybercriminal ecosystem as the principal beneficiary of successful breaches.
cards.source: ENISA — European Union Agency for Cybersecurity
